chapter_theme: Akananuru 101 to 120, in the களிற்றியானைநிரை section: ten paalai poems of roads through raider country, a heroine doubting an old proverb, two mothers grieving for eloped daughters, set beside kurinji night trysts pressed toward marriage, marutham quarrels measured against Chezhiyan's wars, two mullai homecomings and two neythal scenes. Puram names (Ezhini, Evvi, Erumai, Ahthai and the Kosar, Vaanan, Chezhiyan at Koodal) serve as similes and settings for private grief.

101.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the old proverb that no harm comes in this life to those who do good has turned false today, since the man who crossed the many dewy hills, by a vast forest where red-eyed Mazhavar raiders with fire-sticks and bows drive off herds with their calves and where the whirling midday wind shakes the murungai's spent flowers down like cold hail, has gone though she did nothing to deserve his displeasure.
101.nuance: The proverb is about this life (இம்மை), not a reward hereafter: she asks whether right conduct protects anyone now. The image of cool hail made out of flowers shaken down by scorching wind turns the comfort of rain into a sign of heat.

colophon.thurai: பிரிவிடை வேறுபட்ட கிழத்தி, தோழிக்குச் சொல்லியது; தோழி கிழத்திக்குச் சொல்லியதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: she speaks of a man who has crossed the waste and left her

comparisons.tenor: the raiders' curled matted hair, like a ram's horn
the sun crossing the wide sky like a boat
the murungai's spent flowers dropping in the hot wind like cold hail

102.reading: Speaking to her friend so that the hero standing outside will hear, the heroine recalls how the man of the country where a fierce young elephant falls suddenly asleep to a hill girl's kurinji song, while the millet watcher lies drunk on his platform, came softly past the guards through the unbarred door, bees humming on his sandal-smeared chest, embraced her and left with sweet words; and she asks what this pallor is that has now come over her brow along with the gossip, because he has not given her more.
102.nuance: The speech is aimed at the overhearer: the night visit is told as past and tender, the pallor and gossip as the present cost. The fierce elephant lulled by the girl's song and the drunk watchman asleep set a hill where every guard is off duty, which is what made the visits possible; a reader may also hear in the lulled elephant the hero lulled out of his purpose, but no part-by-part match is stated.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக் குறிக்கண் சிறைப்புறமாகத் தோழிக்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தலைமகள் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: a secret night meeting that evades the guards

103.reading: The heroine tells her friend that, thinking the man would have finished his work and come back across the hot, hard waste, past a cattle village whose people have left the tall wide hill, she lay at midnight with pallor as her only companion, and asks whether the one they love will not give back the beauty that went away with him of its own accord.
103.nuance: She does not ask for him but for her beauty, which she says went with him of itself (தம்மொடு தானே சென்ற நலனும்); the deserted cattle village on his road mirrors her own emptied state. Lines 1 to 4 (the spotted cock and what it watches) are obscure in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the shadeless waste the man must cross

comparisons.tenor: the bird's fine spots, as if sprinkled on it

104.reading: The friend blesses the hero who, his king's war finished, drove his swift four-horsed chariot through the cool, bee-loud woodland, leaving behind many small villages where white kids with hollow bellies like empty avarai pods and drooping ears frisk with the children and nibble the aar tree's shoots on the common, and arrived at evening to set flowers in the hair of his bangled wife, who had lived in tears and many reproaches.
104.nuance: The friend praises the return by one act (இனிதுசெய் தனையால்): setting flowers in the wife's hair, the ornament she had given up while he was away. The playful kids of the small villages show the settled domestic life he rides through to reach his own.

thinai_evidence.note: the woodland and the evening of the homecoming

comparisons.tenor: the kids' hollow bellies, like empty avarai pods
the kids' long ears, drooping as if wilted

105.reading: The mother wonders how her daughter, who would not drink the sweet milk her nurses held to her in a jewelled bowl and gave no thought to the family's wealth in their great house cool as a shaded pool, but believed false words, will manage the many-pathed summer journey with the hill man who praises her and weaves her a garland of vengai leaves, through a scorched forest of hot stones where bowmen fulfilling the commission of Ezhini of many spears and the rhythmic-stepping horse drink honeyed toddy and drive off herds of full-uddered cattle across the frontier.
105.nuance: The mother's doubt is about fitness, not morals: a girl who would not even take milk from her nurses now walks a road of cattle raiders. பொய்ம்மருண்டு (deceived by falsehood) is the mother's only judgment of the lover, and the vengai garland he weaves is a hill thing carried into the waste.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's journey away with her man

comparisons.tenor: the family's great house, cool and rich like a shaded pool
the horse's rhythmic steps, like a bouncing ball

106.reading: Hearing that the wife of the man of the bright ford, where an old kingfisher too spent to fly rests on fragrant lotus leaves in a fire-red lotus pond, waiting to eat small fish that leap like popped rice, quarrels with her husband on their account, the courtesan tells her friend that since they cannot escape the blame though they did nothing, they should go there swinging their tight bangles and stroll a little, and let the wife beat her own belly like the drum the bard, who is fed on elephants, beats each time Chezhiyan of the shining-sword army wins a battle.
106.nuance: The courtesan's mockery is in the landscape before it is in her words: the old kingfisher that cannot fly and only waits for the leaping fish is her picture of the wife. Chezhiyan's war drum, beaten at every victory, turns the curse into a public spectacle.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகள் தன்னைப் புறங்கூறினாளாகக் கேட்ட பரத்தை அவட்குப் பாங்காயினார் கேட்பச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulking quarrel over the husband's other women

comparisons.tenor: the red lotus, like flame
the small fish leaping like popped rice
the wife beating her own belly, like the bard's drumhead
the aging wife, too slow to follow her husband among the lively women

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: the courtesan addresses her own friend; the overhearers are the wife's companions

ullurai.tenor: the hero's wife and the young women around her husband, as the courtesan sees them

pairs.situation: the wife, past her youth, can no longer go after her husband
the many lively young women who draw him away
she can only sit at home and sulk

ullurai.speaker_fit: the courtesan is neither heroine nor friend and may use any thing (porul 7.29); the kingfisher and fish are of the marutham pond of the poem

107.reading: The friend tells the hero, who is preparing to leave, that to end the grief she has borne each time she heard of his going, her friend with thick parted hair will go with him: across the hard frontier of the Vadukar, men of strange long speech with fierce dogs who eat white rice cooked with fat on teak leaves, where travelers rejoice at venison a tiger left on the black rock, past the steep slope where a lamed ox left alone is fed iluppai flowers by boys of a hill hamlet who drive the deer off with their bows, she will be his sweet companion at evening, and at dawn the forest will smell like a wedding house as fresh blossoms fall on the gravel.
107.nuance: The friend turns the paalai road into a feast and a wedding: travelers' venison, the Vadukar's rice, a hamlet's evening and a forest that smells like a marriage house. The lamed ox left alone yet fed by strangers stands quietly against the fear of being left behind, though the poem does not draw that sense.

colophon.thurai: தோழி தலைமகள் குறிப்பறிந்து வந்து தலைமகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the hero's departure and the heroine's going with him

comparisons.tenor: the forest at dawn, fragrant as a wedding house

108.reading: Speaking to the heroine so that the hero outside will hear, the friend says that pitying the pain of those one has joined is fitting for those who understand, yet the lord of the cloud-capped mountain, where kaanthal flowers rise like cobras spreading their hoods at a peacock and a bee at their pollen looks like a spinning top, shows no such pity, for he comes alone through midnight dark of pelting rain, where hail struck from an elephant's face streams on the rock like scattered pearls, lightning flashes like sparks of a whirled firebrand, and beasts of prey roam.
108.nuance: The friend turns his courage into a want of kindness (அருளான்): by braving the night path he makes the women suffer fear for him, so true pity would be to stop coming that way, that is, to marry. The snake-hooded kaanthal carries the path's dread into the closing praise of his hill.

colophon.thurai: தலைமகன் சிறைப்புறத்தானாகத் தலைமகட்குச் சொல்லுவாளாய்த் தோழி சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the mountain lord and the midnight tryst

comparisons.tenor: the hailstones scattered on the rock, like pearls at a hill's foot
the hail streaming down the rock, like crystal poured
the lightning, like sparks flying from a firebrand
the kaanthal's flower clusters, like snakes spreading their hoods at a peacock
the bee circling the kaanthal, like a top spun by hand

109.reading: Halfway along the road, the man tells his heart that the town where she lives, she of soft eyes like many-petalled flowers and words as sweet as a well-tuned yazh string, is now cut off by many dry hills: a wide land of tall groves and bamboo where herds of tusk-ploughing elephants gather, forked tracks heaped with countless cairns over men felled by white-tipped arrows, where travelers are killed though they carry nothing, and which a king without aram rules, taking great tusks and striped hides.
109.nuance: Three lines give her, twelve give the road; the killing ground is described so fully that it explains why the hills 'lie across' (விலங்கின) his way back. Lines 11 to 13 (whether the robbers kill to stop witnesses escaping, and whether the king takes tusks and hides as tribute) are hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the waste and the dry hills between him and her town

comparisons.tenor: her eyes, like soft many-petalled flowers
her sweet words, like the sound of a good yazh string

110.reading: Disclosing the secret to the foster mother, the friend says let the mother know and let the gossiping street hear, and swears before the god of the whirling river mouth that there was nothing else: while the girls rested after bathing in the sea, building sand houses and heaping play rice, a man came, said the day was done and he was very tired, and asked whether he might eat with them on spread leaves and stay in their noisy hamlet; they, heads bowed, said the fish food was not fit for him; when the others ran off, crying that a ship with a tall flag was in sight, he looked at her alone and asked, 'Bright-browed one, shall I stay?', and when she said 'go', he stood holding the pole of his tall chariot, gazing — and she says he seems to stand so before her eyes even today.
110.nuance: The friend tells the meeting in her own first person (என்னே குறித்த நோக்கமொடு, என் கட்கே), as if the man had looked at her; whether she speaks for the heroine or shields her by taking the story on herself is left open. The oath before the river-mouth god and the girls' modest refusal (இவைநுமக்கு உரிய அல்ல) are the proofs offered that nothing improper happened.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore games, fish food and ships of the meeting place

111.reading: The friend assures the heroine that the man who crossed the sky-touching hills will not stay content where he is and, ashamed of the scornful words of hostile men, will come back; she pictures his road, where a spider's web on a withered nemai tree swings in the hot wind like the cloth banner on a royal elephant, weary elephants mistake it for a rain-cloud and breathe through their aching trunks like the pipes of performers, and vultures feeding on a boar the red dog has killed show red ears like the lamps carried at night over a battlefield to search out the wounded.
111.nuance: The comfort rests on shame, not longing: he will return because staying away invites scorn. The thirsty elephants deceived by a cobweb into hoping for rain sit uneasily beside a promise of return. Lines 1 to 3 (whose mockery, and why he would be ashamed) can be read more than one way.

thinai_evidence.note: the hot wind and the waste road he travels

comparisons.tenor: the spider's web swinging in the wind, like a royal elephant's cloth banner
the weary elephants breathing through their trunks, like performers' pipes
the vultures' red ears, like lamps searching the wounded on a night battlefield

112.reading: Meeting the hero who has come at night, the friend tells him he has done wrong to come here, not thinking of them alone, through the cold dark grove where at midnight a hunchbacked bear tears open a termite mound and a tiger whose mate is hungry after giving birth kills a tusked elephant and roars; if a day passes without him her friend will not live, and he too desires her embrace, but the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame, so why not marry? Then, not knowing of the union already made, they will watch the ancient rite and see her new shyness like strangers come as guests.
112.nuance: The closing joke turns the secret into a performance: at the wedding the friend will pretend, like a stranger, not to know that the union already happened, and enjoy the bride's shyness. The maxim on the worthy (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்) is the friend's lever.

colophon.thurai: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை யெதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது.

thinai_evidence.note: the night tryst and the friend's demand for marriage

comparisons.tenor: the friend and her circle watching the bride's new shyness, like strangers come as wedding guests

occasion.words: இரவுக்குறி வந்த தலைமகனை யெதிர்ப்பட்டு நின்று தோழி சொல்லி வரைவு கடாயது

iraicchi.act: the tiger, its mate weak and hungry after giving birth, kills a tusked elephant to feed her
iraicchi.sense: even the fierce tiger provides for its mate; the hero, who braves the same dark for stolen meetings, should take her home as his wife and provide for her

113.reading: The heroine tells her friend that the man who joined her shoulders, as rich as the good land of the Kosar (those of many spears who, never swerving from friendship even in bad times, follow and guard Ahthai, giver of elephants), with its neythal fields fragrant of new toddy, abandoned her without kindness while the old town raised its gossip, and is now said to be far off beyond the land of Paanan, past a shrunken stream where enemies who killed travelers washed their weapons; so that her helpless heart may be eased and she can stay without weeping, she wishes her life would leave her body here and go to where he works, as a bird leaves its nest on a swaying branch when the place grows empty.
113.nuance: The Kosar's loyalty 'even in bad times' frames, by contrast, a man who would not stay kind; the body left here like an empty nest is her image of herself. Lines 10 to 16, on the far land and its people, are hard to construe in our text.

thinai_evidence.note: the lover who left and is far away

comparisons.tenor: her shoulders, rich as the Kosar's good land
the rich meats, as if a festival were held

comparisons.vehicle: குடம்பை புல்லெனப் புலம்பெயர் மருங்கிற் புள்எழுந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: her life leaving her body for him, like a bird leaving its emptied nest

114.reading: The returning hero, imagining his wife telling her friend that he does not remember them even in the small dull evening when the weakened sun sinks behind the hill like the moon swallowed by the snake, bids his charioteer, learned in the craft, drive on to end her sorrow: there the tall flags wave on the sky-touching walls of the old guarded town where the watchmen's lamps shine like stars, and they will see the beautiful woman of faultless chastity, with red-streaked rain-dark eyes and shoulders like bamboo.
114.nuance: Lines 1 to 7 are the wife's complaint as the hero imagines it, addressed to her friend (கேளாய், எல்ல! தோழி!); the poem thus holds both voices, hers at home and his on the road. Evening, which makes her grieve, is the hour he races against.

colophon.thurai: வினை முற்றி மீளுந் தலைமகன் தேர்ப்பாகற்குச் சொல்லியது.

thinai_evidence.note: the wet woodland at evening on the way home

comparisons.tenor: the woodland strewn with mixed blossoms, like the ground of the Velan's rite
the setting sun vanishing like the moon swallowed by the snake
the watchmen's lamps on the walls, like stars
her shoulders, like bamboo

115.reading: The heroine tells the friend who urges patience: let the old town of endless festivals gossip though we are blameless, let the harsh-tongued women of the street mock, let my beauty, like the Kudanadu of Erumai of fine ornaments, waste away — only let my lover be free of illness always, he who, bound by the need for wealth, stays far from us across the long road where the konrai's ripe pods, curved like the yazh necks the bards broke off and laid down in worship at the battle where Evvi of the true sword fell, lie strewn on the rock, and where tusked elephants with tusks like the crescent moon hide their herd in fear of a fierce leaping beast.
115.nuance: Her wish is for his health, not his return; she gives up name, mockery and beauty in three concessive clauses (எள்ளினும் எள்ளுக, தொலையினும் தொலைக). The Evvi simile brings a patron's death and the bards' mourning rite into a love poem, so the very pods on his road recall broken harps.

thinai_evidence.note: the man away for wealth and the woman left

comparisons.tenor: her beauty, like Erumai's rich Kudanadu
the konrai's curved ripe pods, like the harp necks laid down by the bards
the elephant's white tusks, like the crescent moon

116.reading: The friend refuses the man of the town of rushing water, where field workers reaping red paddy amid flame-red lotuses prop the toddy cart sunk in the mire with adumpu creepers, telling him he has no shame: people say that yesterday he played in the river with a woman of bright brow, short flower-decked hair, soft eyes and full breasts, at the wide ford where punku flowers open like popped rice; and though they hid it behind lies, the gossip slipped from their hands and grew louder than the shout on the wide field of Koodal when Chezhiyan of the elephant army routed the sea-like hosts of two great kings who had risen together and saw them flee, leaving their drums.
116.nuance: The friend admits the women tried to hide his conduct with lies (பொய்புறம் பொதிந்துயாம் கரப்பவும்), so the refusal is also a confession that the household's loyalty has been spent. The cart sunk in mire and propped with creepers is a scene of the marutham fields; a reader may see the hidden affair being shored up in it, but no part-by-part match is anchored.

thinai_evidence.note: the refusal of the husband over his river-play with another woman

comparisons.tenor: the red lotus, like flame
the opening punku flowers, like popped rice
the two kings' great army, like the sea
the gossip about him, louder than the victory shout at Koodal

117.reading: The foster mother grieves for the girl who, trusting a stranger's false words and forgetting the nochchi that flowers with jasmine and her playmates, left the rich house desolate and went, bangles jingling and anklets ringing on her red feet, through a waste of fearful forked paths where a white-headed kite on a black-stemmed omai calls its mate; she asks whether, since the girl would not let her wash her hair with tagaram when she combed and parted it, that hair, now that her lover as fine as she weaves fragrant flowers into it, falls over her back like the bright ripples of the sweet forest river north of Vaanan's Sirukudi, where a crooked-legged tortoise and its young snatch ripe white mangoes in the encircling pond.
117.nuance: The foster mother's grief is jealous of a task: she combed and dressed the hair the girl would not let her wash, and now pictures the lover doing it. The kite calling its mate on the waste, 'so that pity comes' (அருள்வர), is the pair the girl has become.

thinai_evidence.note: the daughter's elopement through the waste

comparisons.tenor: the lover, equal to the girl in worth
the girl's dark hair falling over her back, like the bright ripples of the forest river

118.reading: The friend tells the hero, who is handsome as Murugan himself, that if he comes by day, his strong hunting dogs behind him, to the small hill village by the roaring white waterfall where women wearing honey-scented vengai flowers dance in the street to the tondakam drum, they fear the gossip, and they fear still more his coming alone at pitch-dark midnight when the tiger that missed the great elephant hurrying with its mate and calf lies in wait; what will become of her friend, who has even stopped singing the parrot-scaring songs in the ripening millet where they met for many days — pitiable, she has nothing but his grace.
118.nuance: Both trysts are closed in turn, day by gossip and night by the tiger, and the millet field is closed too, since she no longer guards it; only marriage is left, though the friend never names it. The elephant that takes its mate and calf out of the tiger's reach is the path's danger here; the poem does not turn it on the hero.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai, the millet field and its parrot-scaring of the hill tryst

comparisons.tenor: the hero, like Murugan

119.reading: Told that he will leave, the heroine (or, in the colophon's second reading, the friend) asks whether the man who looked closely and said 'she will suffer, her brow, shoulders and spotted waist losing colour, beauty and lines', and still goes without thinking marriage good, will truly venture, with a peacock-feathered spear broad-bladed like a neythal petal as his only companion, along a mountain road of dry tracks where pirandai vines cut by travelers wither by the path like the green pieces of a snake struck by thunder, where bow-strong Mazhavar roast meat on the abandoned hearth stones of salt caravans, and where a great elephant whose head the tiger gashed dips its trunk in a dry spring and sighs.
119.nuance: He foresaw her wasting in detail and still did not choose marriage (வரைவுநன்று என்னாது): the complaint is that his knowledge did not change his act. The wounded elephant at the dry spring and the spear as his only companion make the road a place where even strength is alone and thirsty.

colophon.thurai: செலவுணர்த்திய தோழிக்குத் தலைமகள் சொற்றது. தோழி தலைமகட்குச் சொற்றதூஉமாம்.

thinai_evidence.note: the dry road and waterless spring he will take

comparisons.tenor: the cut pirandai withering by the road, like pieces of a thunder-struck snake
the spear's broad bright blade, shaped like a neythal petal

120.reading: Having brought the heroine home from the daytime meeting, the friend tells the hero that the sun has sunk in the west as green-legged herons, flying in a line like the garland on tall Murugan's chest, cross the red sky after fish, and her friend, her proud rain-dark eyes in tears and her fragrant beauty spoiled, has begun to burn with longing; so would anything be lost if, rather than setting out at night with his bowmen and his mule, its leg wounded by a backwater shark and worn out by the long waters, he stayed and then went from their country of the great backwater, where palmyras rise in white-sand gardens, the anril calls and small-budded neythal grows?
120.nuance: The invitation is phrased as a harmless question (சிதைகுவது உண்டோ): staying one night would cost him nothing, while her weeping has already begun. The anril, the bird of pairs that cannot part, calls in the last lines; the poem leaves it as the sound of the place.

thinai_evidence.note: the backwater shore at sunset

comparisons.tenor: the line of herons across the red sky, like the garland on Murugan's chest

links.note: Kural 210 says that ruin is rare for one who does not stray into evil; the heroine of 101 quotes the same rule as an old proverb (நன்றுசெய் மருங்கில் தீதுஇல்) and asks whether it has turned false, since she did nothing hateful and is still left. On her reading the rule has failed.
links.teaches: The pairing shows that the Kural's assurance was already an old proverb in the Sangam age, and that akam poetry was where it was tested: a blameless woman's abandonment is the counter-case the maxim does not answer.

links.note: Purananuru 158 names Ezhini among the seven dead givers, with his horse and sharp spear; Akananuru 105 names Ezhini of many spears with his horse, whose bowmen drive off cattle on the daughter's road. That both mean the same chief is likely but not certain.
links.teaches: The chief keeps the same epithets of horse and spear in both books, but the bard remembers him as a lost giver while the mother sees only his raiders on her daughter's road, so a patron's fame looked different from the path his men made dangerous.

links.note: Both marutham poems bring in Chezhiyan's wars: in 106 the courtesan wishes the wife would beat her own belly like the drum his bard beats at each victory; in 116 the friend says the gossip about the hero's river-play is louder than the shout at Koodal when Chezhiyan routed two kings.
links.teaches: Set side by side they show the Pandya's victories serving both parties to one marutham quarrel, the courtesan's curse and the wife's friend's reproach, so royal war was the common measure of household noise and anger whoever spoke.

links.note: Kural 551 judges the king who harasses his people and does wrong to be crueller than murderers; Akananuru 109 sets the murderers' road, with cairns over men shot though they carried nothing, in hills ruled by a king without aram (அறன்இல் வேந்தன்).
links.teaches: The Kural ranks the bad king against killers in the abstract, while the akam poet already draws the lawless realm and the murderous road as one landscape, so a lover's journey becomes the evidence of what a king without aram costs those who travel his land.

links.note: Kural 657 says the worthy prefer utter poverty to wealth gained under blame; the friend in Akananuru 112 says the worthy, however deep in love, do not want a pleasure that comes with blame (சான்றோர் பழியொடு வரூஉம் இன்பம் வெஃகார்), and so the hero should marry.
links.teaches: The same rule of the worthy, refusing any gain that brings blame, governs wealth in the Kural and love in the Akananuru, and the friend turns it from a counsel of going without into an argument for marriage, which removes the blame without removing the pleasure.

links.note: Same situation: a man held by the king's war who longs to be home at evening. Kural 1268 says let the king fight and win, and we will hold the evening feast with the household; in Akananuru 114 the war is done and the hero urges his charioteer to reach his wife before the evening's grief.
links.teaches: The couplet's two clauses, victory and then the evening at home, become in the poem a race against dusk, and the poem adds what the couplet leaves out: evening is the hour when the waiting wife suffers most, so his haste is to end her sorrow as much as to begin his feast.

links.note: Purananuru 233 is a bard's cry at the dawn news of Evvi's wounds, wishing it false; Akananuru 115 recalls the battle where Evvi fell and, on our reading, the bards breaking off and laying down the curved necks of their harps in worship.
links.teaches: The puram poem gives the bards' words at Evvi's fall and the akam poem their gesture, so together they show that his death was mourned with a known bardic rite that a love poet could cite as an image for seed pods on a road.

links.note: Purananuru 76 praises Chezhiyan, who alone defeated the seven who joined against him; Akananuru 116 recalls Chezhiyan at Koodal routing two great kings who rose together. The battles may not be the same.
links.teaches: Both poets make the Pandya's fame the defeat of an alliance, seven kings in the puram praise and two great kings in Paranar's simile, so one king against a coalition was the shape his fame took, whichever battle is meant.

links.note: Both are paalai laments over a daughter who eloped: in 105 the mother recalls the girl refusing milk from her nurses and caring nothing for the house's wealth; in 117 the foster mother recalls the girl refusing to let her wash her hair, which the lover now dresses.
links.teaches: Read together, the two laments divide the girl's upbringing between the women who raised her, the mother grieving through food and wealth and the foster mother through the hair she tended, and each measures the loss by a care the lover now takes over.

links.note: In 118 the friend closes both trysts, fearing gossip by day and the tiger by night; in 112 she meets him at night, says he did wrong to come through the tiger's grove, and gives the moral ground for marriage.
links.teaches: Taken together they show the friend's case for marriage in two steps: 118 makes every meeting impossible without naming marriage, and 112 names it and supplies the reason a worthy man must accept, that the worthy want no pleasure that brings blame.

new_concepts.gloss: marriage: the formal union that ends secret love, sought or pressed for in the akam poems
new_concepts.label_source: the colophons' word (வரைவு மலிந்தமை, வரைவு கடாயது)

source_issues: 110: line 20 reads பல்லோர் ருள்ளும், a word split by a stray space and doubled consonant; read பல்லோருள்ளும். Line 1 recurs as Akananuru 218 line 18 (a formula).
111: the colophon thurai reads தலைமளை, a misprint for தலைமகளை.
114 and 117: the poet's name is not preserved (the commentary edition prints dots).
118: the colophon thurai breaks off at வரைவு; it presumably ended வரைவு கடாயது.
120: the colophon thurai breaks off after வந்து, without saying to whom the friend speaks; the poem's பெரும (line 9) shows it is the hero.
115: line 7 recurs as Akananuru 227 line 13 (a formula).
103: line 11 was repaired (a stray space before a dead consonant).
